title: One-Word Substitutions
shortDescription: Replacing a whole phrase with a single precise word — grouped by theme so you memorise patterns, not a random list.
genZNote: Why use ten words when a very specific one exists? English hoards a single fancy word for almost every situation.

sections.heading: What this tests
sections.body: A one-word substitution question gives a descriptive PHRASE and asks for the single word that means exactly that — e.g. 'a person who cannot read or write' = ILLITERATE. The skill here is not memorising a giant alphabetical list, but recognising the phrase's underlying THEME (a type of person, a type of place, a type of fear/love, a legal/medical term) so you can narrow down the answer even for an unfamiliar phrase.

rows: One who studies the past through remains
One who is skilled with both hands equally
One who does not believe in God
One who thinks only of themselves
A place where books are kept for reference/borrowing
A place where coins are made

sections.heading: Fear, love, and fields of study (a very high-yield family)
Strategy for unfamiliar substitution phrases
bullets: Identify the THEME first: is the phrase describing a person, a fear, a study, a legal situation? This narrows the likely word family instantly.
Look for a Greek/Latin root hint inside the answer OPTIONS: '-phobia' = fear, '-logy' = study of, '-cide' = killing, '-phile' = love of.
If genuinely unsure, eliminate options that describe only PART of the phrase, not its full precise meaning — one-word substitution answers must match exactly, not approximately.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: One-word substitution replaces a descriptive phrase with the single precise word that captures its exact meaning, usually testable by recognising the phrase's theme and common Greek/Latin word roots.
keyFacts: '-phobia' = fear of, '-logy' = study of, '-cide' = killing of, '-phile' = lover of — recognising these roots unlocks many unfamiliar words.
Group substitutions by theme (people, places, fears, studies) rather than memorising an unordered list.

highYieldFacts: Acrophobia (heights), claustrophobia (closed spaces), hydrophobia (water) are among the most frequently tested phobia words.
Bibliophile (loves books), philanthropist (loves/helps mankind), misanthrope (hates mankind) form a commonly tested contrast set.
commonTraps: Choosing a word that is close but describes only part of the given phrase.
mustRemember: When stuck, decode the root of each option rather than guessing blindly.
possibleQuestions: One word for 'a person who is new to a profession': Novice/Amateur.
One word for 'government by the rich': Plutocracy.
